gold.abstract: Participation incentives is a well-known issue inhibiting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in medicine, as well as a potential cause of user dissatisfaction for RCTs in online platforms. We frame this issue as a non-standard exploration-exploitation tradeoff: an RCT would like to explore as uniformly as possible, whereas each "agent" (a patient or a user) prefers "exploitation", i.e., treatments that seem best. We incentivize participation by leveraging information asymmetry between the trial and the agents. We measure statistical performance via worst-case estimation error under adversarially generated outcomes, a standard objective for RCTs. We obtain a near-optimal solution in terms of this objective: an incentive-compatible mechanism with a particular guarantee, and a nearly matching impossibility result for any incentive-compatible mechanism. We consider three model variants: homogeneous agents (of the same "type" comprising beliefs and preferences), heterogeneous agents, and an extension that leverages estimated type frequencies to mitigate the influence of rare-but-difficult agent types.

We integrate conjoint-derived utilities for AD trial-design attributes with adaptive-trial taxonomy to test whether adding a low-utility convenience feature (car service) concurrently distorts enrollment without improving speed. Using [paper-c]’s utility weights as behavioral inputs, we simulate prospective versus concurrent adaptation and assess enrollment time, severity drift, and type I error. This extends [paper-c] from static preference measurement to dynamic trial-design validation and gives paper-b a preference-based mechanism for population drift.

transcript.C|1:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper A (computational social science) contributes a validated method for detecting coordinated inauthentic behavior (CIB) in online networks using temporal posting-pattern clustering. Paper B (cognitive psychology) contributes a controlled experimental paradigm showing that exposure to repeated false statements increases perceived truth (illusory truth effect), mediated by processing fluency.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
CIB clusters repeatedly propagate identical or near-identical false claims across accounts. This repetition is operationally equivalent to the repetition manipulation in Paper B’s paradigm. The causal chain proposed: coordinated repetition → increased processing fluency in target audiences → inflated truth judgments. The missing cross-paper link is whether coordinated repetition (not just incidental repetition) produces fluency-driven belief change in real social media contexts; no source paper tests this.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Phase 1: Apply Paper A’s clustering method to a public social media dataset to identify CIB clusters and extract repeated false statements. Phase 2: Adapt Paper B’s paradigm into a 2×2 online experiment: repetition source (coordinated cluster vs. organic diverse accounts) × statement repetition (once vs. five times). Measure truth ratings (Paper B scale), processing fluency (self-report ease-of-processing, Paper B), and perceived source diversity. Validate CIB detection against manual annotation; validate fluency mediation using Paper B’s mediation procedure. Hypotheses: coordinated repetition increases truth ratings more than organic repetition, mediated by fluency, controlling for prior familiarity.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
This project tests whether coordinated inauthentic repetition of false claims increases belief via processing fluency. We combine a computational method for detecting coordinated clusters with an experimental paradigm for illusory truth. By experimentally manipulating repetition source (coordinated vs. organic) and frequency, we isolate the causal effect of coordination on truth judgments. The contribution is a mechanistic account of coordinated disinformation effects, bridging network-level detection and individual-level cognition, beyond either paper’s scope.

FINAL IDEA: Coordinated inauthentic repetition of false claims increases perceived truth through processing fluency, testable by pairing computational cluster detection with an illusory-truth experiment.

Paper B (cognitive psychology) provides an experimental paradigm showing repeated false statements increase perceived truth via processing fluency. Researcher B’s proposal uses only Paper C (conjoint analysis for AD trial design), so no paper-grounded contributions are adopted from it; its simulation-based forecasting idea is rejected as an integration mechanism because it lacks a second source paper.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Coordinated repetition (Paper A) produces high-frequency, near-identical message exposure. This is causally parallel to the repetition manipulation in Paper B. The missing cross-paper link is whether repetition originating from coordinated clusters (vs. organic diverse sources) differentially increases processing fluency and truth judgments. Hypothesis: coordinated repetition increases truth ratings more than organic repetition at equal frequency, mediated by fluency, because coordinated clusters reduce perceived source diversity and increase message uniformity.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Phase 1: Apply Paper A’s clustering method to a public dataset (e.g., Twitter/X) to identify CIB clusters and extract repeated false claims. Validate clusters against manual annotation and account-level metadata. Phase 2: 2×2 between-subjects online experiment (N=800): repetition source (coordinated cluster vs. organic diverse accounts) × repetition frequency (1 vs. 5 exposures). Participants view a feed with target false statements embedded among filler posts. Measure truth ratings (Paper B scale), processing fluency (Paper B self-report ease-of-processing), and perceived source diversity (manipulation check). Test mediation: source → fluency → truth rating, controlling for prior familiarity and political alignment. Pre-register analysis; use Paper B’s mediation procedure.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether coordinated inauthentic repetition of false claims increases belief via processing fluency. Combining a computational method for detecting coordinated clusters with an experimental paradigm for illusory truth, we manipulate repetition source (coordinated vs. organic) and frequency. The contribution is a mechanistic account of coordinated disinformation effects, linking network-level coordination to individual-level cognition, beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: Coordinated inauthentic repetition of false claims increases perceived truth through processing fluency, testable by pairing computational cluster detection with an illusory-truth experiment that isolates source coordination as the causal factor.
